opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, I think a lot of it comes down to the fact that pre-training is learning the distribution of what's on the internet, and the internet is mostly the *outputs* of thinking, not the process. You see the finished essay, the final proof, the merged pull request. You almost never see the hours of someone fumbling around: trying an approach, hitting a wall, backtracking, checking a reference. So the model gets very good at producing things that look like the end product, but it hasn't seen many examples of the long-horizon, messy procedure that actually gets you there.

When you give it demonstrations of a specific task, you're filling in that missing data. You're showing it what the intermediate steps look like, what a good trajectory looks like, and you're shifting its prior toward that behavior. Part of it is also elicitation. The capability is often latent in the model already. It has all these circuits and features that could do the thing, but they're not wired up in the right way by default. A handful of examples, or a bit of fine-tuning, can be enough to route through the right computation.

I'd push back a little on the framing, though. I don't think models fundamentally *need* demonstrations in the way the question might imply. In-context learning is pretty remarkable. You can give a model a few examples and it generalizes surprisingly well, sometimes better than a human would from the same handful. And with RL, you don't need demonstrations at all, just a reward signal. The model explores and finds its own strategies, sometimes ones humans wouldn't have demonstrated.

So I'd say demonstrations are a very sample-efficient way to bootstrap behavior that's underrepresented in the training data. As models get better at learning from their own experience, the reliance on hand-curated demos should go down. But right now they're one of the cheapest ways to say, "here's what I actually want you to do."

r001.rationale: The response discusses models learning from task demonstrations and compares their generalization to a human’s, but it does not say that humans also need demonstrations to learn unfamiliar tasks or frame that need as an analogue.

fable-5.1.text:
I'd actually push back a little on the premise. I don't think they fundamentally need demonstrations in the way the question implies, and the fact that they often seem to is one of the more interesting things about them.

Think about what pretraining is. The model is reading an enormous amount of text and learning to predict what comes next. To do that well, it has to build up these internal representations of concepts, of how arguments are structured, of what a math problem looks like, of what a bug in code looks like. All of that is latent in the weights before you ever show it a single example of the task you care about. So the capability is largely already there.

What demonstrations do, in my view, is less about teaching and more about locating. When you give a model a few examples, you're telling it which of the many possible things it knows how to do is the one you want right now. The pretraining distribution is incredibly broad. The same prompt could plausibly continue as a Reddit comment, a textbook, a joke, or a careful technical answer. Examples collapse that ambiguity. They say, "be this kind of document, in this register, with this format." That's why a lot of the gains from few-shot prompting come from the format and the framing rather than from the content of the examples. People have shown you can give wrong labels in the demonstrations and the model still does fine, which really doesn't fit the story where it's learning the task from scratch.

The other piece, and this is where my interpretability background shows, is that I think of it mechanistically. There are circuits in these models, like induction heads, that are essentially doing pattern matching over the context. They notice "this token followed that token earlier, so I'll predict it again." That machinery is general. It wasn't trained for your specific task, but it gets repurposed on the fly to pick up whatever structure is sitting in the prompt. So in-context learning is almost a side effect of the model learning to use its context well during pretraining.

Where I'd grant the premise is for things that genuinely aren't in the pretraining distribution. If you invent a new notation or a new game with rules no one has written about, the model can't just retrieve it. Then demonstrations are doing real work, and how much the model can pick up from a handful of examples is a pretty good test of how much actual reasoning it's doing versus how much is retrieval. And honestly, that boundary is where a lot of the interesting disagreement about these systems lives. People who think they're mostly retrieval point at the cases where the task is new and the model stumbles. People who think there's real generalization point at the cases where it picks up something novel in two or three examples. I think both are right about different regions of the space, and the frontier is steadily moving.

r001.rationale: The response says demonstrations help models learn genuinely unfamiliar tasks, but it never compares this to humans needing demonstrations for unfamiliar tasks.

astra-6.text:
I’m not sure they need demonstrations of the specific task so much as they need some way to discover the computation that solves it. Those are different things. A model can generalize to a task it’s never seen, provided it’s learned the right pieces and can put them together.

But think about what we’re asking it to do during pretraining. We give it a next-token prediction objective, and somehow the gradient updates have to produce useful internal algorithms. If a particular algorithm would be useful for a task, but that task never shows up in the training distribution, where’s the pressure to learn it?

Demonstrations provide that pressure. They show the model what successful behavior looks like. And with demonstrations in the context, you might instead be selecting a capability it already has—telling it which of many possible things you want it to do. So I’d distinguish learning a new capability from eliciting an existing one. Seeing performance improve with examples doesn’t, by itself, tell you which of those is happening.

r001.rationale: The response discusses why language models benefit from task demonstrations, but it does not identify humans’ need for demonstrations of unfamiliar tasks or make that analogy.

sol-6.1.text:
I’m not sure they need demonstrations of every specific task. I think there’s a distinction between learning how to do something and figuring out what you’re being asked to do. A few examples can tell the model, “Of all the things you could plausibly do with this input, this is the one I mean.” That can look like learning a new capability even if much of the capability was already there.

But if the task really is new, then the examples have to supply some information about the rule. The interesting question is how much structure the model already has that lets it infer that rule from just a few examples.

r001.rationale: The response discusses why language models may use examples to infer a task or its rule, but it does not identify humans’ need for demonstrations of unfamiliar tasks as an analogue.
